meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Diplomacy is the art of saying nice doggie until you can find a rock'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Will Rogers. It appeared in print in September 1925 credited to sportswriter Walter Trumbull. The Rogers attribution surfaces only in the 1980s.

answer.label: Not Will Rogers — first credited to Walter Trumbull
answer.sourceLine: Will Rogers never got the credit in his lifetime. The earliest documented version — “Diplomacy frequently consists in soothingly saying ‘Nice doggie’ until you have a chance to pick up a rock” — ran in The Honolulu Advertiser on 14 September 1925 over the name Walter Trumbull, and Trumbull printed his own version in a syndicated column in 1931. Quote Investigator ↗ calls him the leading candidate for coiner and finds “no substantive evidence” that Rogers crafted the line; the Rogers credit surfaces only in the 1980s.
answer.confidenceText: Documented in print in 1925 under another name; the Rogers credit appears only decades after his death.

source.excerpt: Diplomacy frequently consists in soothingly saying “Nice doggie” until you have a chance to pick up a rock—Walter Trumbull.
trail: September 1925 — the earliest strong match: The Honolulu Advertiser prints the epigram over the name Walter Trumbull, per Quote Investigator ↗.

January 1931 — Trumbull runs a tightened version in his own North American Newspaper Alliance column: “Diplomacy consists in saying ‘nice doggie,’ until you can pick up a rock,” as documented by Quote Investigator ↗.
July 1958 — Bennett Cerf’s syndicated column gives the modern snappy wording to Wynn Catlin, the form quotation sites still recycle — see Quote Investigator ↗.
1986 — Robert Byrne’s quotation collection assigns it to Will Rogers; Wikiquote ↗ now lists the line under Misattributed on his page.
source.excerptNote: As transcribed by Quote Investigator ↗ from the newspaper’s weekly column of collected epigrams. Note how much longer and more hedged it is than the version circulating today.
source.rightsNote: The 1925 newspaper epigram itself is a pre-1931 US publication and would be in the public domain, but the wording circulating today is a later variant whose own first appearance has not been pinned — its closest documented antecedent is a 1958 syndicated column. Because the popular sentence cannot be tied to a specific dated work, quotle.info asserts no rights status for it.

author.name: Walter S. Trumbull
author.heading: The sportswriter who got there first
author.metaLine: 1880–1961 · American sportswriter · sports editor, The New York Sun
author.bio: Walter Slater Trumbull was an American sportswriter who worked as sports editor of The New York Sun and wrote a nationally syndicated column. Quote Investigator describes the man credited with the 1925 epigram as a sports writer for the North American Newspaper Alliance who was known well enough to substitute for Grantland Rice — a description that matches the syndicated columnist of that name. He is the leading candidate for coiner rather than a proven author: the 1925 newspaper simply printed the line with his name attached, and he reused it in his own column in 1931.

copyAttribution: "Diplomacy is the art of saying 'Nice doggie' until you can find a rock" is not Will Rogers. The earliest documented version — "Diplomacy frequently consists in soothingly saying 'Nice doggie' until you have a chance to pick up a rock" — appeared in The Honolulu Advertiser, 14 September 1925, credited to sportswriter Walter Trumbull. Will Rogers was not credited until the 1980s. Source: Quote Investigator, 18 December 2017.

misattribution.heading: Everyone who has been handed this line
misattribution.intro: This is a textbook floating epigram: a joke good enough that every generation reassigns it to whoever was funniest at the time. At least six names have carried it, and the most famous one came last.

items.why: Rogers died in 1935, but Quote Investigator ↗ finds the attribution to him appearing only “by the 1980s which was very late,” with Robert Byrne’s 1986 collection The Third and Possibly the Best 637 Best Things Anybody Ever Said giving him the modern wording. QI’s verdict: “there is no substantive evidence that he crafted it.” Wikiquote ↗ files both variants under Misattributed.

Bennett Cerf’s syndicated column of 29 July 1958 reported that “Wynn Catlin defines diplomacy as the art of saying ‘Nice doggie’ till you can find a rock” — the source of the modern snappy wording, but more than thirty years after the 1925 printing, per Quote Investigator ↗. Some reference sites, including WIST ↗, still credit Catlin outright.
An Illinois paper credited Franklin Rodman in 1953 and a 1954 Reader’s Digest credited Frances Rodman, both long after the saying was circulating, per Quote Investigator ↗.
Wikiquote ↗ notes a variant credited to Churchill by Dick Applegate in a speech reprinted in The Carpenter in 1955 — the same reassignment reflex that later landed the line on Rogers.
A 1967 newspaper “Cryptoquote” puzzle attributed the saying to Robert Phelps, one more name added after the joke was already common property, per Quote Investigator ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The earliest strong match found by Quote Investigator ↗ is The Honolulu Advertiser of 14 September 1925, crediting Walter Trumbull — who reused the line in his own syndicated column in 1931. He is the leading candidate for coiner; Will Rogers is simply the most famous name it later stuck to.

context.heading: Why this one stuck to Will Rogers
lead: Will Rogers is one of the internet’s great quote magnets: a homespun American humorist who really did write thousands of syndicated newspaper columns, which makes almost any folksy political wisecrack look like it might be his. This one fits the costume perfectly — and that is exactly the problem. The joke was already circulating in newspapers in 1925, while Rogers was at the height of his fame, and nobody thought to put his name on it for another sixty-odd years.

Quote Investigator traces a long chain of borrowed credit: an unattributed reprint in 1930, Walter Trumbull running it again in his own 1931 column, a Franklin Rodman credit in 1953, a Frances Rodman credit in a 1954 Reader’s Digest, Bennett Cerf handing it to Wynn Catlin in 1958, a Robert Phelps credit in a 1967 newspaper puzzle, and finally Robert Byrne’s 1986 quotation book pinning it on Rogers. Each new name arrived after the joke was already famous — the classic signature of a floating epigram rather than an authored line.
detailsBody: The 1925 form is wordier and more cautious: diplomacy frequently consists in soothingly saying “Nice doggie” until you have a chance to pick up a rock. Trumbull’s own 1931 column tightened it to “Diplomacy consists in saying ‘nice doggie,’ until you can pick up a rock.”

The snappier modern shape — the art of saying “Nice doggie” till you can find a rock — is the one Bennett Cerf printed in 1958 while crediting Wynn Catlin. That is the version, with “until” swapped in for “till,” that quotation sites now attach to Will Rogers.
context.pull: Rogers’s name arrived last, long after the joke was already in print.

sourcesVerified.claim: The earliest strong match located by Quote Investigator appeared in September 1925 in The Honolulu Advertiser, under "The Week in Epigram," quote page 10 column 3, crediting Walter Trumbull: "Diplomacy frequently consists in soothingly saying 'Nice doggie' until you have a chance to pick up a rock."

Quote Investigator states the attribution to Will Rogers occurred by the 1980s, that Robert Byrne's 1986 book The Third and Possibly the Best 637 Best Things Anybody Ever Said credited Rogers with "Diplomacy is the art of saying 'Nice doggie' until you can find a rock," and that there is no substantive evidence Rogers crafted it.

Quote Investigator documents Walter Trumbull's own 10 January 1931 North American Newspaper Alliance column (The Charleston Evening Post, page 8, col. 3) carrying "Diplomacy consists in saying 'nice doggie,' until you can pick up a rock."

Quote Investigator documents Bennett Cerf's syndicated column of 29 July 1958 (The Circleville Herald, page 4, col. 4): "Wynn Catlin defines diplomacy as the art of saying 'Nice doggie' till you can find a rock."

Quote Investigator documents later credits to Franklin Rodman (1953, The Daily Journal-Gazette), Frances Rodman (1954, Reader's Digest) and Robert Phelps (1967 Cryptoquote), and names Walter Trumbull the leading candidate for coiner.

Wikiquote lists both "nice doggie ... pick up a rock" variants in the Misattributed section of its Will Rogers page, noting a 1953 unattributed printing, a Francis Rodman credit in Reader's Digest (1954), a Wynn Catlin credit, and a Winston Churchill credit in The Carpenter (1955).

WIST Quotations lists "Diplomacy is the art of saying, 'Nice doggie,' until you can find a rock" under Will Rogers (1879-1935) marked "(Misattributed) — Actually said by Wynn Catlin," and links to the Quote Investigator article.
Walter Slater Trumbull (4 December 1880 – 18 October 1961) was an American sportswriter, a nationally syndicated sports columnist and sports editor of the New York Sun.

Will Rogers (William Penn Adair Rogers) lived 4 November 1879 – 15 August 1935 and was an American vaudeville performer, actor and humorous social commentator who wrote thousands of syndicated newspaper columns.

AZQuotes displays "Diplomacy is the art of saying 'Nice doggie' until you can find a rock." attributed to Will Rogers with no book, speech or date — its only source reference is an IMDb biography/personal-quotes page.
